analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate drug prices, lets individuals import drugs from Canada, and bans pay-for-delay deals.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to three House committees in September 2015, sent to a Health subcommittee, and died there when the 114th Congress ended, with 18 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the government to negotiate prescription drug prices on behalf of everyone in Medicare's drug program, closed the Medicare 'donut hole' coverage gap three years early, and required drug makers to pay rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare and Medicaid patients. It also would have let individuals and pharmacies import cheaper drugs from Canada, banned 'pay-for-delay' deals in which brand-name drug makers pay generic competitors to stay off the market, stripped a drug maker's exclusive marketing rights if it committed fraud, and required drug companies to disclose what they spend on research, marketing, and how they price drugs abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people in Medicare's drug program would pay less at the pharmacy: the government would negotiate prices for them, and the coverage gap known as the donut hole would close in 2017 instead of 2020. Low-income Medicare and Medicaid enrollees would benefit from required manufacturer rebates. Patients generally would benefit from earlier access to cheaper generics, the option to import drugs from Canada, and new transparency about how drug prices are set.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, Medicare and Medicaid enrollees, and drug buyers

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Health and Human Services would be required to negotiate prices (including discounts and rebates) with drug manufacturers for drugs covered under Medicare Part D, replacing the current 'noninterference' rule under which the government may not negotiate [S2][S3].

The bill accelerates closing the Medicare Part D donut hole from 2020 to 2017 and raises the manufacturer rebate in the gap from 50 percent to 75 percent, so beneficiaries would stop paying the full cost of their drugs sooner [S2][S3].

Drug manufacturers would have to pay the government a rebate, similar to Medicaid's, for each drug dispensed to low-income Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries; makers that refuse would have their drugs excluded from Medicare drug coverage [S2][S3].
The Medicaid additional rebate requirement would be extended to generic drugs, increasing rebates for a program that serves low-income patients [S2][S3].

Individuals would be allowed to import prescription drugs from Canada, and pharmacists and wholesalers would be allowed to import as well, potentially from other countries — giving patients access to the same drugs at foreign prices [S2][S3].

'Pay-for-delay' settlements — in which a brand-name drug maker gives a generic competitor anything of value to stay off the market — would be presumed anticompetitive and enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission, letting cheaper generics reach patients sooner [S2][S3].

A drug maker that commits fraud, illegal marketing, or misbranding — or fails to report it — would lose its period of market exclusivity on that drug, so competitors could bring cheaper versions to market sooner [S2][S3].

Drug makers would have to report publicly each year what they spend on research, clinical trials, manufacturing, and marketing for each drug, plus their profits, Federal benefits received, and prices and sales in foreign countries [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost: lower Medicare prices through negotiation, new rebates on drugs for low-income beneficiaries and on generics under Medicaid, a bigger donut-hole rebate, loss of exclusivity when they commit fraud, a ban on paying generic makers to delay competition, and public disclosure of pricing and spending data. Medicare drug plan sponsors would face new reporting duties with fines for late or false information.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows individuals to import drugs from Canada and potentially other countries; critics have long argued that a wider importation channel raises the risk of counterfeit or improperly handled medicines reaching patients, which is why the bill requires the Health Secretary to write regulations first [S2][S3].

Even the negotiation requirement has limits an honest supporter would acknowledge: the bill expressly bars the Secretary from imposing a particular formulary, which reduces the government's leverage and could make the negotiated prices weaker than mandatory negotiations in other countries [S3].

The bill imposes new compliance and reporting burdens — Medicare drug plan sponsors face civil fines of $10,000 per day for late data and up to $100,000 per false item, and manufacturers must produce detailed annual pricing and spending reports [S3].

The FDA and brand-name industry have traditionally argued that cutting U.S. drug prices or exclusivity could reduce incentives to develop new medicines; this bill does not address that trade-off directly, it simply prioritizes lower prices and earlier generic competition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and broad: tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries would pay less for drugs, low-income patients would gain rebates, and all consumers would gain from earlier generics and legal importation from Canada. The costs fall almost entirely on brand-name drug manufacturers' profits and on some administrative burden for plan sponsors. The safety risk of individual importation is real but addressed through regulation, and the negotiation requirement is softened by the ban on mandating a formulary. On balance, this is a bill whose costs fall on a concentrated industry and whose benefits spread widely across patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced it was sent to three House committees and then a Health subcommittee, and none of them ever brought it up before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2015 in the House on September 16, 2015 [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — on the day it was introduced [S5].
Two days later, on September 18, 2015, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].
The bill had 18 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they kept Medicare paying un-negotiated prices, paid no new rebates on low-income beneficiaries or generics, kept their pay-for-delay settlements, and faced no loss of exclusivity for fraud or public disclosure of pricing data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and their shareholders

sides.party_line_note: All 19 House members who backed the bill were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it, and the three committees it was referred to were all chaired by Republicans, who took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to negotiate Medicare drug prices, pay Medicaid-style rebates for low-income beneficiaries and added rebates on generics, raised donut-hole rebates from 50 to 75 percent, stripped market exclusivity after fraud convictions, banned pay-for-delay payments, and required public disclosure of pricing and spending. Their revenues would have fallen directly, and those revenues come largely from prices paid by patients and public programs.

The pay-for-delay ban would have let them launch cheaper generics years earlier by blocking settlements that pay them to stay off the market. The new Medicaid additional rebate on generic drugs, however, would have cut their revenue on that program.

industries.industry: Medicare drug plan insurers and plan sponsors
industries.note: Their enrollees would have paid less for drugs as negotiated prices and bigger rebates flowed in, and plan sponsors could still negotiate further discounts below the government price. They would also have taken on new reporting duties with fines of up to $10,000 per day for late data.

The bill would have explicitly allowed importation of prescription drugs from Canada — and potentially other countries — by wholesalers and pharmacists as well as individuals, opening a lower-cost supply channel.
